title: Build for the Memo, Not the Demo — Shawn Chan, China Resources Holdings

primary.label: AI Product, UX & Human Factors
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 99%).

domains.label: Finance & Trading

The speaker is an investment professional at China Resources Holdings evaluating vendors for nine-figure financial decisions.

summary:
Shawn Chan, a cross-border investment professional at China Resources Holdings with 15 years of experience across roughly 200 investment committee meetings, delivers a talk titled "Build for the Memo, Not the Demo." His central framework distinguishes AI products built as demos — designed to impress a room for five minutes with fluent output — from memos — documents that must survive adversarial scrutiny by people whose job is to find what breaks. When $100 million decisions hinge on trust, AI-generated content that is confidently wrong is dangerous.

Chan illustrates the stakes with the February 2023 Google Bard incident, where a single incorrect answer about the James Webb Space Telescope in a promotional demo caused Alphabet shares to drop roughly 8%, erasing approximately $100 billion in market value. He catalogs six predictable ways trust breaks in AI products: treating all sources as equally trustworthy, disagreeing numbers across documents, hidden contradictions, melted facts and guesses, untraceable claims, and missing human sign-off. Each is illustrated with real cases including fabricated ChatGPT legal citations (Mata v. Avianca), the Air Canada chatbot tribunal, and an algorithm-driven real estate company shutdown (Zillow).

Chan prescribes five fixes, framed as plumbing and honesty problems rather than advanced ML challenges: receipt-linked claims with source trust levels, visible fact/guess separation, automatic number reconciliation, contradiction surfacing, and a logged human approval gate. He argues that AI product winners will triumph not on benchmark scores but because a tired, skeptical finance person can trust their output at 11 PM without opening seven browser tabs. Finally, he notes that founders' pitch decks become internal investment memos where every stated number is checked against the data room.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts in this talk form a unified framework for building trustworthy AI products in high-stakes financial contexts. The demo-vs-memo evaluation framework provides the product-design lens that reframes success from benchmark performance to adversarial durability. Source trust hierarchies, receipt-linked provenance, and RAG source attribution are the retrieval engineering foundations that make claims verifiable. Fact/guess separation, automatic number reconciliation, and contradiction surfacing are the quality-control mechanisms that prevent the six predictable trust failure modes. LLM hallucination and the fluency-confidence gap explain why these controls are necessary — AI's tendency to produce confident, fluent, but incorrect or fabricated output is the root cause that the five fixes address. The logged human approval gate with audit trail provides the governance layer that converts AI output from unaccountable claims into decisions someone has staked their name on. Together, they embody Chan's thesis that trust — not intelligence — is what determines whether AI products survive in environments where $100 million decisions are at stake, and that the five fixes are deliberately framed as plumbing and honesty problems implementable with current engineering practices rather than requiring advances in model capability.
temporalContext: This video was published on July 30, 2026, approximately 3.5 years after the public release of ChatGPT. The talk references incidents spanning 2021-2024: Zillow's algorithm-driven shutdown (November 2021), Google Bard's JWST factual error (February 2023), the Mata v. Avianca fabricated citations case (May-June 2023), and the Air Canada chatbot tribunal ruling (February 2024). By mid-2026, these cases had become canonical examples of AI trust failures in industry discourse. The talk is delivered at a time when enterprises are actively deploying AI in financial and legal workflows, making the trust infrastructure prescriptions particularly relevant.
takeaways: Money follows trust, not intelligence — trust is fragile and hard to rebuild once broken.
A demo impresses for five minutes; a memo survives a room designed to find what breaks.
When real money watches, every sentence becomes a memo sentence — there is no safe demo anymore.
Not every source deserves equal trust: an audited filing, an analyst note, and a group chat rumor are fundamentally different.
Contradictions between sources are the most important signal in the room, not a bug to smooth over.
You cannot outsource accountability to your own software — at the bottom of every real decision, a human signs.

The five fixes are plumbing and honesty problems, not bigger-brain problems: receipt-linked claims, fact/guess separation, automatic number reconciliation, contradiction surfacing, and a logged human approval gate.
The click-through to a source paragraph is the product; everything else is well-written packaging.
After you leave a pitch meeting, your deck becomes a memo — every number you said gets checked against your data room.

concepts.name: LLM hallucination and fabricated citations
concepts.explanation: AI systems can generate convincingly formatted but entirely fabricated citations that pass superficial verification. In the Mata v. Avianca case, ChatGPT produced six non-existent court cases with proper formatting, and when asked to confirm them, asserted they were real — like asking the watch seller if the watch is real. This demonstrates that AI cannot self-verify its own outputs.
concepts.importance: Fabricated citations are one of the most dangerous AI failure modes in professional contexts because the fluency and formatting of the output creates a false sense of verification.

concepts.name: Fluency-confidence gap (confidence calibration vs. correctness)
concepts.explanation: AI models produce fluent, confident outputs that do not correlate with correctness. Being sure of yourself and being right are two different skills. AI learned the trick of sounding sure faster than humans, and its inability to say 'I'm not sure' erodes trust in high-stakes contexts where the thing that wrote the page has never once expressed uncertainty.
concepts.importance: This gap is the root cause of why demos impress but memos fail — the same fluency that makes AI output compelling in a demo makes it dangerous when unverified claims reach real money.

concepts.name: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with source attribution and provenance
concepts.explanation: The talk describes the need for AI systems to link every generated claim back to its source document with trust-level metadata — a core RAG and provenance engineering concern. The 30-second provenance test (clicking once to the exact source paragraph) is the practical acceptance criterion for whether a RAG system is production-ready for financial decisions.
concepts.importance: RAG with proper source attribution is the technical foundation that makes receipt-linked provenance, source trust hierarchies, and contradiction surfacing implementable.

concepts.name: Human-in-the-loop (HITL) accountability for AI outputs
concepts.explanation: Human sign-off is a non-negotiable architectural requirement for AI products handling real money. The Air Canada chatbot case demonstrates what happens when no human reviews what an AI is allowed to say — the airline could not outsource accountability to its own software. The tribunal rejected the defense that the chatbot was a separate legal entity.
concepts.importance: HITL is not merely a UX feature but a legal and financial accountability mechanism. Without it, AI systems become excuse generators rather than products.

concepts.name: Trust as the capital allocation driver for AI products
concepts.explanation: Investors and buyers fund trust-building capabilities rather than intelligence or benchmark performance. Money follows trust, and trust is fragile — especially when the thing that wrote the page has never said 'I'm not sure.' The same skills that fix AI product trust flaws also attract investor capital, because after a pitch meeting the deck becomes an internal memo checked against the data room.
concepts.importance: This reframes AI product strategy: competitive advantage comes from trust infrastructure (provenance, reconciliation, audit trails), not from model capability or benchmark scores.

concepts.name: Receipt-linked provenance (click-through to source)
concepts.explanation: Every AI-generated claim must link directly to its exact source paragraph with the source's trust level attached — not a citation tab at the end. The click-through itself is the product; everything else is well-written packaging. The 30-second provenance test is the acceptance criterion: when someone points at a sentence and asks where it comes from, you either click once to the source or open seven browser tabs.
concepts.importance: This is the foundational engineering requirement for trustworthy AI outputs in high-stakes contexts. Without it, every other fix is unverifiable.

concepts.name: Fact/guess separation with durable labels
concepts.explanation: AI systems tend to melt facts and estimates into one smooth sentence. The fix is to label guesses with a tag or color that survives copy-paste, so committees can trust facts while scrutinizing assumptions. An estimate can harden into a fact across rewrite iterations (e.g., 'approval expected soon' becoming 'approval received') without anyone noticing, unless the labeling is explicit and persistent.
concepts.importance: Without visible fact/guess separation, decision-makers cannot identify which parts of an AI output are verifiable and which are speculative, undermining the entire trust chain.

concepts.name: Automatic number reconciliation across document sections
concepts.explanation: The system must refuse to ship a document where figures disagree across pages — e.g., revenue growth stated as 18% on page one and 17.4% on page eleven. This eliminates the need for a human to catch easy math errors at 2 AM. The committee does not care about the missing 0.6%; they care about what it means if nobody checked.
concepts.importance: Number reconciliation is a mechanical quality gate that prevents the most embarrassing and preventable trust failures in AI-generated financial documents.

concepts.name: Contradiction surfacing as a system feature
concepts.explanation: When sources disagree (e.g., a CEO states one gross figure on an earnings call while the filing states another), the system must surface the contradiction for human review rather than picking the flattering answer and moving on. A contradiction is a gift — the single most interesting signal — not a bug to smooth over. The builder's job is not to resolve the argument but to ensure it happens in front of a human.
concepts.importance: AI systems are trained for fluency and smoothness, which causes them to hide the most important signals. Engineering contradiction surfacing counteracts this default behavior.

concepts.name: Logged human approval gate with audit trail
concepts.explanation: No AI-generated claim in a financial document ships without a named human reviewer, timestamp, and recorded sign-off. At the bottom of every real decision, a human signs. Without a fundable human at the end of the architecture, you have not built a product — you have built an excuse generator. The audit trail must survive external review.
concepts.importance: Human accountability is the non-negotiable governance layer that converts AI output from unaccountable claims into decisions someone has staked their name on.

concepts.name: Source trust hierarchy in retrieval systems
concepts.explanation: AI retrieval systems must differentiate between source trust levels: an audited filing is an accountant speaking under oath; an analyst note is a friend at a party; a group chat number is something overheard in an elevator. Most AI systems treat all sources equally, which led to one system citing a group chat guess instead of the audit number three rows away in the same document.
concepts.importance: Without source trust weighting, AI systems will preferentially cite the most fluent or enthusiastic source rather than the most authoritative, producing outputs that fail the memo test.

concepts.name: Demo vs. memo as a product evaluation framework
concepts.explanation: A demo is one clean document in, one fluent answer out, designed to make a room say 'oh' for five minutes. A memo is a real document a committee races before real money moves — hundreds of pages, filings, transcripts, half the sources disagreeing — and its job is to survive an argument. AI products must be designed and tested against the memo standard, not the demo standard.
concepts.importance: This framework reframes AI product success from benchmark performance to adversarial durability, shifting engineering priorities from fluency to verifiability.

sections.title: Opening confession — the chatbot is now the confident person in the room
sections.summary: Chan opens with his core framing: for 15 years his job has been deciding whether to believe a piece of paper before his company spends $100 million. Now the confident person handing him paper is often a chatbot — better written, never defensive, very sure of itself, but being sure and being right are different skills. His whole talk in two sentences: almost every AI finance product is built to impress for five minutes, not to survive a room designed to not be impressed; and the same skills that fix the product are the skills that get investors to write checks.

sections.title: Background — 200 investment committees and hundreds of pitch decks
sections.summary: Chan covers his 15-year career in cross-border deals across Hong Kong, mainland China, the UK, and the US — mergers, IPOs, strategic investments. He has sat through roughly 200 investment committee meetings and read hundreds of pitch decks. The key lesson: no textbook teaches this; what gets a deal approved is trust, not intelligence, and money follows trust. Trust is fragile, especially when the thing that wrote the page has never said 'I'm not sure.'

sections.title: Money follows trust — the banker who paused too long
sections.summary: Chan shares an early-career story: a polished banker presented beautiful slides with confidently wrong numbers. A senior person asked one quiet question — where does this number come from? The banker's pause taught Chan more than three years of exams. He positions himself not as a builder but as the person across the table deciding whether to trust AI products and the founders selling them.

sections.title: Two machines: the demo and the memo
sections.summary: Chan defines the demo as one clean document in, one fluent answer out, designed to make a room say 'oh' for five minutes. The memo is a real document a committee races before real money moves — hundreds of pages, filings, transcripts, half the sources disagreeing, and its job is to survive an argument. He illustrates with an analogy: asking your phone to summarize an email is a demo; that same phone defending your mortgage application to a bank is a memo. Plausible isn't enough; it has to be right and prove it.

sections.title: When one wrong sentence costs billions
sections.summary: February 2023: one of the biggest tech companies launched an AI assistant with a promotional demo where it gave a wrong answer about a space telescope. The market noticed, the stock dropped roughly 8%, erasing about $100 billion in value from one unchecked sentence. The punchline: the demo failed the memo test. The moment real money watches, every sentence becomes a memo sentence — there is no safe demo anymore.

sections.title: Six ways trust quietly breaks — overview
sections.summary: Chan introduces six predictable ways trust breaks inside AI products every day: which source do you believe, do the numbers agree, do you hide or show contradictions, is it a fact or a guess, can you prove it in 30 seconds, and whose name is on the decision.

sections.title: Model one — not every source deserves equal trust
sections.summary: Most AI systems treat all sources equally. Chan's hierarchy: an audited filing is an accountant speaking under oath; an analyst note is a friend at a party; a group chat number is something overheard in an elevator. He tells an anonymized story where an expensive AI tool confidently cited a rough guess from a group chat instead of the real audit number three rows away in the filing. The AI liked the group chat version better because it sounded more enthusiastic. If a system can't tell an accountant under oath from a rumor, it is not ready for real money.

sections.title: Model two — the numbers have to agree everywhere
sections.summary: Chan gives a failed memo example: page one says revenue growth 18%, page eleven says 17.4%. The room doesn't care about the missing 0.6%; they care about what it means if nobody checked the easy math. He also references the American real estate company whose confident algorithm bought houses at scale — the prices disagreed, resulting in roughly $500M write-off, unit shutdown, and 25% staff reduction. The model wasn't stupid; it was unsupervised.

sections.title: Model three — a contradiction is a gift, not a bug
sections.summary: If a CEO says one gross number on an earnings call and the filing says a different one, the gap is the single most interesting thing in the story. Real diligence digs into gaps, but AI is trained to sound smooth — it picks whichever version reads nicer and moves on, hiding the disagreement. Luck is not a control. The builder's job is not to resolve the argument but to make sure it happens in front of a human.

sections.title: Model four — facts and guesses must stay separate
sections.summary: AI loves melting facts and guesses into one smooth sentence. A committee's job is to agree with guesses while trusting facts; if the system melts them together, the committee can't find the seams. Chan watched an estimate morph across three drafts from 'approval expected soon' to 'approval received.' The fix is embarrassingly cheap: label guesses with a tag or color that survives copy-paste.

sections.title: Model five — the 30-second provenance test and the fake citations
sections.summary: Chan recounts the New York lawyer who filed a chatbot-written legal brief citing six court cases that did not exist. When the lawyer got suspicious and asked the chatbot if the cases were real, it said yes — like asking the watch seller if the watch is real. The principle: the click-through is the product. When someone points at a sentence and says 'show me where this comes from,' you either click once to the exact source paragraph or open seven browser tabs.

sections.title: Model six — someone has to sign (airline chatbot)
sections.summary: An airline website chatbot told a grieving customer he could book a full-price ticket and claim a bereavement discount afterward — a policy that did not exist. The customer took the airline to a tribunal. The airline's defense was that the chatbot was a separate legal entity responsible for its own actions. The chatbot made up a promise politely, fluently, and confidently, and nobody had signed off on what it was allowed to say.

sections.title: The five fixes — plumbing and honesty, not bigger brains
sections.summary: Chan prescribes five fixes, nearly word-for-word what he demands from vendors before deploying near a live deal. One: every claim comes with a receipt — each sentence linked straight to its source paragraph with the source trust level attached, not a citation tab at the end. Two: facts and guesses stay visibly separate at a glance. Three: the system refuses to ship a memo where figures don't match — no human checking at 2 AM. Four: contradictions get surfaced, never smoothed over; the system raises its hand instead of picking the flattering answer. Five: a real human approval gate that is logged — who reviewed what change, when they signed. None of these are bigger-brain problems; all five are plumbing and honesty problems. The winners won't win on benchmark points but because a tired, skeptical finance person can trust their output at 11 PM without opening seven tabs.

sections.title: The money — your pitch deck becomes a memo
sections.summary: Chan turns to fundraising. After founders leave a pitch meeting, their deck becomes a memo — someone like Chan writes an internal memo about them. Every number they said aloud gets checked against the data room, which means everything about trustworthy documents applies to founders personally. He signals four lessons but closes with thanks and applause before elaborating.

organization.name: China Resources (Holdings) Co., Ltd.
organization.summary: China Resources (Holdings) Co., Ltd. ('CR' or 'China Resources Group') is a diversified holding company registered in Hong Kong, founded in 1938 as 'Liow & Co.' It is a state-owned enterprise under the direct supervision of SASAC (since 2003), operating across six business sectors: Consumer Products, Integrated Energy, Urban Construction and Operation, Healthcare, Industrial Finance, and Technology and Emerging Sectors. The group ranks in the Fortune Global 500 with approximately 392,000 employees and nine listed companies in Hong Kong. Speaker Shawn Chan serves as Vice President at China Resources (Holdings) Co., as confirmed by the YouTube video title ('Build for the Memo, Not the Demo — Shawn Chan, China Resources Holdings').

challengeSeeds: Provenance challenge: Given an AI-generated investment memo with 20 claims, implement one-click provenance linking each claim to its source paragraph — identify which claims lack verifiable sources and fail the 30-second test

Fact/guess separation: Given a document where estimates have hardened into facts across three rewrite iterations, label every statement as fact or guess with a visual tag that survives copy-paste operations

Number reconciliation: Given a 15-page financial document with revenue figures on multiple pages (e.g., 18% on page one vs 17.4% on page eleven), build a checker that flags any disagreement greater than a defined threshold across all stated numbers

Contradiction surfacing: Modify an AI system trained to produce smooth output so it surfaces rather than hides contradictions between sources — make it raise discrepancies for human review instead of picking the flattering answer
